name: Schedule page
description: What is planned and when, drawn with time as the axis: promised deliveries across a month, production against each line, a shift roster. Position carries meaning — further right is later, and a block twice as wide takes twice as long.
when_to_use: The screen a planner opens to find out whether Tuesday is over-committed — delivery dates promised across a month, production planned against each machine, a shift roster, a maintenance calendar. The first boundary to draw is against calendar, because half of this screen looks exactly like it and is not it. calendar is a date picker: a month grid whose whole job is to return one date or one range into a field, whose cells are options, whose selected day is a value about to be posted, and which closes the moment the answer is given. Nothing on this page is being picked. The cells carry records, the grid is a view of data rather than a control, there is no field under it and no value to commit — a day here is somewhere you go, not something you choose. A screen that puts a month on it so that somebody can fill in Required by is calendar/picker inside form-page, and reaching for this entry because the month grid looked similar hands the user a schedule they cannot type a date into. The trap is sharpest at calendar/marked, which draws dots on days and is still a picker: its dots are a hint about the day you are about to select, and its cells are still buttons that answer a form. If the grid returns a value, it is calendar. Against index-page: the same deliveries as a register — sortable, filterable, pageable, exportable, with the promised date as one column among nine — and that is the better answer whenever the question is which rather than when. Which orders are late, which vendor is worst, what is outstanding against a cost centre: register. Whether Tuesday can take another truck: this. Against board: columns by stage, not by time. A board's axis is how far a record has got, its columns are a process, and moving a card between two of them is a state change on the server; here nothing moves between columns, a block moves along the axis because a date changed, and the axis is a measurement rather than a set of buckets. Where a Thursday block is not later than a Wednesday one but merely different, the layout is a board and this one is lying about its own geometry.
rules: Position is the message, and everything else follows from that. A block's left edge is when it starts and its width is how long it lasts, so a block cannot wrap to a second line, cannot be reordered for tidiness, and cannot be given a minimum width that would make a two-hour job look like a four-hour one. Every rule below is that one rule meeting a case where it is inconvenient.

The geometry is a percentage of the track and not a count of columns. A block is absolutely positioned inside a relative lane with left and width in per cent, which is the same style attribute progress writes its fill with. Snapping blocks into a grid of fixed cells is the version that ships first and it rounds every start time to the nearest cell — 06:20 becomes 06:00, three of those in a row become an hour of production that does not exist, and the screen stops being a measurement.

The month grid gives up the proportional axis on purpose, and that is the one place it is allowed. At a month's scale the unit is the day: a delivery is promised on the 18th, not at 46.9 per cent of the 18th, and drawing a stripe across three cells to mean a three-day job would need the grid to be a matrix rather than a table of days. What a month grid answers is how many and on which day; the hour is what week, day and resource are for, and the view switcher is how the planner gets from one question to the other.

Monday first, matching calendar, and for the same reason: every Indian office runs Monday to Saturday and a Sunday-first grid puts the weekend at both ends of the row. Saturday is a working day and is drawn white like any other; Sunday is the recessed fill. A plant holiday is a third thing again and it is not the national calendar — 15 August closes every plant in the country and the annual maintenance shutdown closes this one, so both are marked and only one of them is a public holiday. A schedule that renders the gazetted list and calls it the factory calendar promises deliveries into a shutdown.

A block is the chip token and nothing new: bg-zinc-200, ring-1 ring-inset ring-zinc-300, hovering to zinc-300. Colour lives in the 6px dot exactly as it does in badge, so a month of blocks reads as a month of work with six late ones in it rather than as a heat map. A field of red behind a block is the defect the alert rule already names, and on a screen where forty blocks are visible at once it is worse than anywhere else.

A block truncates and never wraps, and what survives the truncation is decided rather than left to the browser. The record number is first and always fits; the vendor name is what goes, then the times, then the quantity, and the order is the same on every view so a planner learns it once. A block narrower than its own number shows the dot and no text, carries the whole record in its accessible name, and hands the pointer to hovercard — an unreadable half-number is worse than a bare bar, because a bar does not look like an answer. There is no minimum width, ever: a block widened to fit its label draws forty minutes as two hours, which is the one thing this layout may not do.

Two things at one time have to be visibly at once. Overlapping blocks on one lane split the lane's width and sit side by side, so the overlap is a shape on the screen rather than a sentence somewhere else. Stacking them into separate rows is the arrangement that hides the one fact the planner opened the page for.

Three different nothings, and they must not look the same. A day inside the published plan with nothing on it is white and empty — silence means nothing is booked. A day past the planning horizon carries one zinc-500 line saying so, because an empty cell and an unplanned cell are the difference between a free Wednesday and a Wednesday nobody has looked at. A non-working day is the recessed fill with its reason written in it. Draw all three as blank cells and the planner books a truck into a shutdown.

Over-commitment is a mark beside a figure, never a coloured lane. A line booked past its shift shows the hours as booked of available and an alert-triangle in amber-700, which is board's limit rule unchanged, and the block that runs past the end of the shift is clipped at the edge of the lane with its right corners squared so the clip reads as an overrun rather than as a block that happens to end there.

A day holding more than fits shows the first three and a control that expands the cell in place. An anchored panel was rejected twice over: a panel opened inside a grid cell is clipped by whichever scroller the grid sits in, which is board's reason for putting its stage list in normal flow, and at 390px there is nothing to anchor one to. Expanding in place grows the week row, which is honest — that week does have more in it.

The resource grid is the only region here that scrolls sideways, it does it inside its own overflow-x-auto box, and it exists only from md up. Below that the same rows are a stacked list with the times written out, which is table's sticky-column rule and this layout does not get to opt out of it: a matrix that scrolls sideways on a phone is indistinguishable from a layout that broke.

Everything on the grid is a link and nothing is dragged. Moving a delivery is a date change on a record with a reason attached to it, which is a form and not a gesture; a schedule whose only way to reschedule is dragging a block is a schedule that cannot be operated with a keyboard, on a tablet, or by anyone who needs to say why the date moved. The block opens the record and the record is where the date is changed.

The period, the view and the scope all belong in the URL. A planner sends a colleague the Silvassa extrusion week of 17 August, and every one of those three has to survive the paste; write them with history.replaceState if they are changed without a reload. Which day is expanded does not go in the URL — it is not a fact about the schedule.

The snippet root is a bounded frame — h-[640px], rounded-xl, border-zinc-300 — so a whole screen previews in a box. As a real page it renders inside app-shell's <main>: drop the wrapper's height and border, keep the mx-auto max-w-[1600px] gutter on the band and on the grid so the h1 and the first column line up, and let the sticky ruler stick to the shell's scrolling column.

anatomy.description: page-header's <header> inside <main>: white, edge to edge over a border-zinc-200 rule, its content in the same mx-auto max-w-[1600px] gutter the grid uses. Holds the trail, the one h1, the scope line and the page's actions.
The role="status" under the h1 saying what is on screen — how many are planned in this period, how many are late, what they are worth. Rewritten by the period, the view and every filter.
Previous, the period label, next, and Today. calendar's chevron buttons unchanged, with the label as an aria-live region so paging is announced rather than silently redrawn.
Month, Week, Line and Day as a <nav> of anchors on button-group's segmented track, the current one carrying aria-current="page". Four URLs, not four panels.
The row or column of labelled hours that names the axis. Sticky against the grid's own scroller, and aria-hidden — the hours are decoration, and every block carries its own in its name.
The relative track one resource or one day owns. Blocks are positioned inside it in per cent; it never shrinks below the height of the blocks stacked in it.
One scheduled thing: the chip fill, a status dot, the record number, and as much else as the width allows. A link to the record, never a drag handle.
The "+2 more" button on a day that holds more than fits. Expands the cell in place; the same button collapses it.
The booked-of-available figure on a resource row, with an amber-700 alert-triangle when booked exceeds available. Advisory — the schedule still accepts the work.
bg-zinc-50 with its reason in it — Sunday, a public holiday, a plant shutdown. Three different reasons and the same fill, because the difference is in the words.
The part of the grid past the planning horizon, carrying one line saying nobody has planned it yet. Distinct from a planned period that happens to be empty.
The dot key under the grid, from calendar's marked variant: what each status dot means, once, rather than a tooltip per block.
What the grid becomes at 390px: one day at a time, the time in a gutter, the blocks as rows, and the gaps written out as sentences.
One removable chip per filter in force, on the recessed band under the band, with the count of what is hidden in the scope line.

behaviour: Paging the period redraws the grid and rewrites the scope line, and does not move the view, the scope or the vertical position. Today returns to the period containing today and puts focus nowhere — it is a jump, not a selection.
A block is a link to its record. Opening one leaves the schedule where it was; nothing on this page edits a date in place, because a date that moves needs a reason recorded against it.

A day holding more blocks than fit shows three and a control. Pressing it expands that cell, grows the week row and swaps the control to Show less; only one day is expanded at a time, and the expansion is not in the URL.
Overlapping blocks on one lane split its width and both stay legible. The lane grows to hold whatever is stacked in it rather than clipping the second one.

A block that runs past the end of its lane is clipped at the edge with its right corners squared and says by how much in its own text. The capacity figure on the row goes to booked-of-available and takes the amber mark.

A delivery promised on a non-working day is drawn on that day rather than moved to the next working one. Moving it silently is how a plant discovers on the morning of the shutdown that four trucks are on their way.

Filtering hides blocks and never moves one. Every count on screen becomes n of m while any filter is in force, the scope line says how many are hidden and by how many filters, and the figures revert to the plain form when the last chip goes.

The resource grid scrolls sideways inside its own box from md up, with the resource column sticky against the left edge. Below md it is a stacked list, and nothing on the page scrolls sideways at any width.
At 390px the grid is gone and the day is an agenda: one day, a time gutter, the blocks as rows in order, and the gaps stated as sentences rather than drawn as space.
accessibility: One <main>, one <h1> in the band, and every region below it an h2 — the month, each resource lane, the agenda for a day. The heading outline is the shape of the plan.

The month grid is a real <table> with th scope="col" for the weekdays, the same as calendar, and the difference is inside the cell: calendar's cell is a button that returns a value, and this one holds a <ul role="list"> of links to records. Row and column position is available without sight either way.

The geometry is decoration and every block says so. A lane is not readable, so each block carries its resource, its start and its end in an sr-only span inside the link — a span rather than an aria-label, so the visible text stays a prefix of the accessible name and the name a speech user says out loud is the one written on the screen. The one block that takes an aria-label instead is the one too narrow to show any text at all, where there is no visible label for the name to contain.
The ruler is aria-hidden. Reading twelve hour labels before the first block is noise, and the hours are already in every block's name.

The period label is aria-live="polite" so paging is announced. The scope line is a separate role="status" that is in the document from first paint, and the two never speak at once — paging does not change the scope and filtering does not change the period.
Today carries aria-current="date" on the day number, which is a fact about the calendar and not about any record on it.
A non-working day says why in real text inside the cell, never by fill alone. A recessed cell with nothing in it is a day that reads as free to everyone who cannot see the fill.
The overflow control names what it would reveal and what day it is on — "Show 2 more on 18 August" — because "+2 more" repeated four times down a month is four controls with the same name.
A block that is clipped by the edge of its lane says so in its text, not by being cut off. A visual clip is not information to a screen reader and the overrun is the whole point of that block.

Each resource lane is a <section> named by its own h2, and its capacity figure is inside that section, so a block announced out of context still has a resource and the row it belongs to still has a name.

Every chip's remove button names the filter it drops — "Remove the filter Extrusion", never "Remove" — and clearing all of them moves focus to the scope line, which is tabindex="-1" for exactly that and is also the sentence saying what happened.

variants.name: What a block shows at four widths
variants.html:
The scheduled block

One lane, 06:00 to 22:00. Every block below is the same record at a different duration.

What the text does

  • A fortnight, or the whole lane

    MS-4838 06:00 – 22:00 · 16.0 h Injection 120T · 9,500 crates · Meera Joshi

    Number, times, duration, resource, quantity, owner. Everything the record has that a planner reads at a glance.

  • Half the lane — eight hours

    MS-4838 06:00 – 14:00 · 9,500 crates Injection 120T, Meera Joshi

    The owner and the resource drop out of the block; the lane already names the resource and the record page holds the rest.

  • Two hours

    4838 MS-4838, Injection 120T, 06:00 to 08:00, 9,500 crates, Meera Joshi

    The prefix goes before the digits do. MS- is the same on every block on the screen; 4838 is the one part that identifies this one.

  • Forty minutes

    The dot and nothing else, with the whole record in the accessible name. Widening it to fit the number would draw forty minutes as two hours, which is the one thing this layout may not do.

What the edges do

  • Started before this lane began

    MS-4835 Started 21:00 yesterday · ends 11:30

    Square on the left, rounded on the right, and the start date written in. A rounded left edge at 06:00 says the job started at 06:00.

  • Runs past the end of the shift

    MS-4838 14:00 – 23:30 · runs 1.5 h past shift end

    The overrun is in the text as well as in the clip, and the lane it sits on carries the amber mark on its booked-of-available figure.

  • Two on one lane at one time

    MS-4835 · 06:00 – 14:00 MS-4841 · 12:00 – 20:00

    The lane grows and the two blocks keep their true left and width, so the overlap is a shape. Squeezing both into one row hides the two hours that are the whole problem.
